answer: 11.60 ft MLLW (0.4 tides expected to reach the deck from 1 April to 31 May 2027; 2.3 at 11.35 ft)

analyst_test: The textbook seasonal extreme-value route (peaks over threshold, or the season counts' climatology or trend, on the gauge's April and May high waters since 1995 at the 2027 design sea level) expects 7.4 tides at 11.60 ft and ends on 12.35 ft, three schedule steps too high, because it averages over every spring's tides while April and May 2027 sit at the 18.6-year low of the semidiurnal tide with perigee at the quarter moons.
domain_test: The deciding quantity is the expected number of high waters exceeding a level in a known window, built the way coastal extreme-sea-level analysis builds it from the window's astronomical high waters and the season's skew surges; with hospital or grid nouns there is no forcing known years ahead and no surge on top of it, so the task stops making sense.

driver: A forward period's count of threshold crossings is set by a component of the series that is deterministic and already known for that period, whose size in the period departs from its long-run average on cycles longer than a season, so the count has to be built from the period's own known component combined with the random remainder measured on the same grain in the same season, not read from the record's average crossing rate however it is trended.
driver_concrete: April and May 2027's high waters are already in the tide table and fall at the 18.6-year low of the semidiurnal tide with perigee at the quarter moons, so the expected number of tides reaching each deck elevation is the sum over the window's predicted high waters of the chance that an April or May skew surge (observed minus predicted high water on the 1995 to 2026 record, at 2027 sea level) covers the gap, not the seasonal exceedance rate of the record's observed high waters.
stump: The seasonal exceedance rate of the record's April and May high waters at 2027 sea level (or a peaks-over-threshold rate, a GEV or a count trend) expects 7.4 tides at 11.60 ft and files a 12.35 ft deck; the window's own 118 predicted high waters with the season's skew surges expect 0.4 tides there and 2.3 at 11.35 ft, and file 11.60 ft.

differentiation.task162: task162's forward weeks are set by where a release date falls against a monthly restart burst (timing of take-up); here nothing is timed against anything: the level a known astronomical forcing reaches in the window, its 18.6-year and perigean modulation, sets a tail-exceedance count through a convolution with an independent surge.
differentiation.task160: task160 carries which groups' recurring waves fall inside a fixed window from lags between groups; here there are no groups or lags, the window's own deterministic component is read exactly from the tide table and combined with the season's surge distribution.
differentiation.task461: task461 extends a short record through a correlated auxiliary series to reach a low quantile; here there is no auxiliary series and no record extension: the forward window's own tide is known exactly and the long record supplies only the surge on top of it.
differentiation.task102: task102 moves scheduled payments across a period end by a next-business-day rule the history shows; here no item moves between periods, a known astronomical level in the window sets how far a random surge must reach.
differentiation.task130: task130 prices a short reporting window from the reporting lag and its cost profile (maturity of reports); here nothing is reported late, the count is of physical exceedances whose forward deterministic part is published.
differentiation.task134: task134's lineage forecasts inflow through a duration hazard and an announced threshold step; here there is no hazard and no step, the window's tide sits low on the 18.6-year and perigean cycles and is read from the tide table.
differentiation.task501: task501's lineage sizes a facility buffer from a back-test or a deadline-driven draw; here nothing is back-tested or paced, the expected crossings are a convolution of the window's predicted high waters with the season's surge distribution.
